about: Manawydan brings the captured mouse home in his glove, and over Cigfa's protest that it is beneath a man of his rank, he means to hang it. On the Mound of Arberth he sets up a little gallows, and three travellers come by in turn, the first people he has seen in Dyfed in seven years: a poor scholar, a priest, and a bishop with his retinue. Each begs him not to demean himself and offers to buy the creature, the price rising from a pound to horses and packs. Manawydan refuses every price until the bishop tells him to name his own. He asks for Pryderi and Rhiannon to be freed, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance. The bishop is Llwyd son of Cil Coed, who laid the spell to avenge Gwawl; the mouse is his pregnant wife. Everything is restored, and the branch ends by explaining its name.

sentences.t: Dyuot y'r ystauell yn yd oed Kicua, a goleuhau y tan, ac wrth y llinyn dodi y uanec ar y wanas a oruc.
sentences.l: Coming to the chamber where Cigfa was, and lighting the fire, and by the string putting the glove on the peg he-did.
sentences.i: He came to the chamber where Cigfa was, lit the fire, and hung the glove by its string on a peg.
sentences.n: The part runs straight on from the last: Manawydan has reached the court with the mouse tied up in his glove. Three verbal nouns (Dyuot 'coming', goleuhau 'lighting', dodi 'putting') are closed by one a oruc 'he did', which makes all three finite: he came, lit, put. y'r 'to the': Evans writes the two together (y2 ystauell); they are divided as in the second witness. yn yd oed 'in which was', where she was: yd is the particle before the vowel of oed. Kicua is Cigfa (k = c, u = f). goleuhau 'kindle, light' (golau + -hau). wrth y llinyn 'by the string': in the manuscript this y is written above the line; it is brought into the line. y uanec ← manec 'glove', softened after y (the feminine article, or 'his'). ar y wanas ← gwanas 'peg, support', softened after the article (the noun is feminine).

sentences.t: “Beth yssyd yna, Arglwyd?” heb y Kicua.
sentences.l: “What is there, Lord?” said Cigfa.
sentences.i: “What have you there, Lord?” said Cigfa.
sentences.n: Beth 'what' ← peth 'thing', the softened form used as the question word. yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. yna 'there'. Arglwyd 'Lord' in address. heb y Kicua 'said Cigfa': heb y is used before a name, heb ef, heb hi before a pronoun.

sentences.t: “Lleidyr,” heb ynteu, “a geueis yn lledratta arnaf.”
sentences.l: “A-thief,” said he-for-his-part, “that I-got stealing on-me.”
sentences.i: “A thief,” he said, “that I caught stealing from me.”
sentences.n: Lleidyr … a geueis 'a thief … that I caught': the object comes first, then the particle a and the verb. This is the abnormal sentence, the ordinary order of Middle Welsh narrative, and it stresses nothing. geueis ← keueis, 1 sg. preterite of kaffael 'get, catch', softened after a. heb ynteu 'said he for his part' (house: 'he said'). yn lledratta 'stealing': yn with a verbal noun. arnaf 'on me', ar conjugated (1 sg.). One steals 'on' a person, that is, from him.

sentences.t: “Pa ryw leidyr, Arglwyd, a allut ti y dodi y'th uanec?” heb hi.
sentences.l: “What kind-of thief, Lord, could you put in your glove?” said she.
sentences.i: “What kind of thief, Lord, could you put into your glove?” she said.
sentences.n: Pa ryw 'what kind of': ryw softens the noun after it, so lleidyr > leidyr. a allut 'that you could' ← gallut, 2 sg. imperfect of gallu, softened after a; ti repeats 'you'. y dodi: y 'him' as the object before the verbal noun, 'his putting', that is, to put him. dodi would soften to /ð/, but this spelling writes /d/ and /ð/ alike, so nothing shows. y'th uanec 'into your glove': y stands for yn 'in' before 'th 'your', and 'th softens manec. heb hi 'said she', with plain hi.

sentences.t: “Llyma oll,” heb ynteu, a menegi ual yr lygryssit ac y diuwynyssit y grofdeu idaw, ac ual y doethant y llygot idaw y'r grofd diwethaf yn y wyd.
sentences.l: “Here-is all,” said he-for-his-part, and telling how had-been-spoiled and had-been-ravaged the crofts to-him, and how came the mice to-him to the last croft in his presence.
sentences.i: “Here is the whole of it,” he said, and he told how his crofts had been ruined and laid waste, and how the mice had come to the last croft before his eyes.
sentences.n: Llyma oll 'here is all'. a menegi 'and telling': after the speech, a verbal noun carries the story on. lygryssit ← llygryssit, impersonal pluperfect (-ssit) of llygru 'spoil': 'had been spoiled'. The yr before it is unusual. It may be the particle y with the perfective particle ry run together, and ry softens, which would explain lygryssit. That is not certain, but the Red Book has the same yr before the verb, so it is not a slip of this scribe. The next verb has the plain particle: y diuwynyssit 'had been ravaged', from diuwyno 'despoil, spoil'. grofdeu 'crofts', plural of grofd, written with g as the scribe's own form of the word (see the last part). idaw 'to him', y conjugated (3 sg. masc.): 'his crofts', and in the next clause 'came on him'. y doethant 'came', 3 pl. preterite of dyuot. yn y wyd 'in his presence' ← gwyd, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “Ac un ohonunt oed amdrom, ac a deleis, ac yssyd yn y uanec, ac a grogaf inheu auory. Ac ym kyffes y Duw, bei as caffwn oll, mi a'y crogwn.”
sentences.l: “And one of-them was very-heavy, and that I-caught, and that-is in the glove, and that I-will-hang I-for-my-part tomorrow. And by my confession to God, if I-could-get-them all, I it-is-that would-hang-them.”
sentences.i: “And one of them was heavy, and that one I caught, and it is in the glove, and tomorrow I shall hang it. And on my oath to God, if I could catch them all, I would hang them.”
sentences.n: ohonunt 'of them', o conjugated (3 pl.). oed amdrom 'was very heavy' (am- + trom, as in the last part). ac a deleis 'and that I caught': deleis is the 1 sg. preterite of dala; its d would soften after a, but the spelling cannot show it. ac yssyd 'and that is'. a grogaf ← krogaf 'I will hang', 1 sg. present with future sense, softened after a. inheu 'I for my part'. auory 'tomorrow'. ym kyffes y Duw 'by my confession to God', an oath. ym is 'my' (uy); the nasal mutation of kyffes (nghyffes) is not written here, but it is in uyghyffes (38). bei 'if', from the imperfect subjunctive of bot. as is the preverbal particle a carrying the infixed pronoun 's 'them' (bei a's). caffwn 'I could get', 1 sg. imperfect subjunctive of kaffael. mi a'y crogwn 'I would hang them': 'y is the infixed object 'them'; crogwn, 1 sg. imperfect, here with a conditional sense.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb hi, “diryued oed hynny. Ac eisswys anwymp yw guelet gwr kyuurd, kymoned, a thidi, yn crogi y ryw bryf hwnnw. A phei gwnelut iawn, nyt ymyrrut yn y pryf, namyn y ellwng e ymdeith.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said she, “no-wonder was that. And yet unseemly is seeing a-man of-equal-rank, of-equal-birth, with you-yourself, hanging that kind of creature. And if you-did right, you-would-not-meddle with the creature, but its loosing away.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” she said, “that would be no wonder. And yet it is unseemly to see a man of your rank and birth hanging a creature of that sort. If you did right, you would not meddle with the creature, but let it go.”
sentences.n: diryued 'no wonder' (di- + ryued); oed 'was' carries the sense 'would be' here. eisswys 'yet, nevertheless', so written in the White Book; the Red Book has eissoes. anwymp 'unseemly': an- 'un-' + gwymp 'fine, fitting', softened in the compound. gwr kyuurd, kymoned, a thidi 'a man of equal rank, of equal birth, with you': ky- 'equal' + urd 'rank', and kym- + boned 'lineage', the b of boned lost into the m of the prefix (kyf- + b > kym-). a thidi 'with you yourself': a 'with', then tidi (the emphatic doubled pronoun) with the spirant mutation after a. The phrase recurs below. y ryw bryf hwnnw 'that kind of creature' ← pryf, softened after ryw. pryf is any small beast, vermin (modern pryf 'insect, worm'). A phei ← pei 'if', spirant after a. gwnelut 'you did', 2 sg. imperfect subjunctive of gwneuthur. nyt ymyrrut 'you would not meddle' (ymyrru, modern ymyrryd). namyn 'but'. y ellwng 'its loosing' ← gellwng, softened after the masculine y 'its'; it agrees with pryf. e ymdeith 'away'.

sentences.t: “Meuyl ymi,” heb ef, “bei as caffwnn i wy oll, onys crogwn ac a geueis, mi a'e crogaf.”
sentences.l: “Shame to-me,” said he, “if I-could-get-them I them all, if-I-did-not-hang-them; and what I-got, I it-is-that will-hang-it.”
sentences.i: “Shame on me,” he said, “if I could catch them all and did not hang them; and the one I have caught, I shall hang.”
sentences.n: Meuyl ymi 'shame to me' (house: 'shame on me'); ymi is y 'to', 1 sg. bei as caffwnn i wy oll: Evans has caffwnn, with nn, and the words are divided caffwnn i as in the second witness (the letters are the same). The Red Book reads pei as caffôn i oll ôwynt. wy 'them' takes up again the infixed -s 'them' in as, so the pronoun is said twice, once infixed and once free. onys crogwn 'if I did not hang them': ony 'if not' + 's 'them'. ac a geueis 'and what I caught': a used as a relative with no antecedent. mi a'e crogaf 'I will hang it': 'e is the infixed object, the same pronoun that is spelt 'y in 5.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb hi, “nit oes achaws y mi y uot yn borth y'r pryf hwnnw, namyn goglyt ansyberwyt y ti. A gwna ditheu dy ewyllus, Arglwyd.”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord,” said she, “there-is-not cause to me to-be a-help to that creature, but guarding-against un-courtesy to you. And do you-for-your-part your will, Lord.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” she said, “I have no reason to stand up for that creature, except to keep you from discourtesy. So do as you will, Lord.”
sentences.n: Ie 'Yes' (house). nit oes 'there is not'. achaws 'cause, reason'. y mi 'to me'. y uot 'to be' ← bot, softened after y 'to'. yn borth 'a help, a support' ← porth, softened after the predicative yn. goglyt 'guarding against, avoiding' (modern gochel). ansyberwyt 'un-courtesy' (house: l 'un-courtesy', i 'discourtesy'). gwna 'do', 2 sg. imperative of gwneuthur. ditheu ← titheu 'you for your part': a pronoun after the verb is softened. dy ewyllus 'your will'.

sentences.t: “Bei gwypwn inheu defnyd yn y byt y dylyut titheu bot yn borth idaw ef, mi a uydwn wrth dy gynghor am danaw; a chanys gwnn, Arglwydes, medwl yw genhyf y diuetha.”
sentences.l: “If I-knew I-for-my-part a-reason in the world that you-ought you-for-your-part to-be a-help to-it, I it-is-that would-be by your counsel about-it; and since I-do-not-know-it, Lady, a-mind is with-me to-destroy-it.”
sentences.i: “If I knew any reason in the world why you should stand up for it, I would follow your counsel in the matter; but since I know none, Lady, I mean to destroy it.”
sentences.n: Bei gwypwn 'if I knew': gwypwn is the 1 sg. imperfect subjunctive of gwybot. defnyd 'matter, reason'. y dylyut 'that you ought', 2 sg. of dylyu. idaw ef 'to it' (y, 3 sg. masc.). mi a uydwn 'I would be' ← bydwn, 1 sg. imperfect of bot, softened after a. wrth dy gynghor 'by your counsel' ← kynghor, softened after dy. am danaw 'about it' (am, 3 sg. masc.). a chanys gwnn: the sense requires 'since I do not know it', so chanys is best read as kan 'since' + nys 'not … it' (with the spirant after a 'and'). The same word is plain canys 'since' in 75, so the spelling allows either reading, and here only the negative makes sense. Compare Kanys gollyngy in 55, where the Red Book writes the two words out, kan nys. Here the Red Book has a chanys nys gwnn, canys 'since' with the negative nys written separately, so the White Book may instead have lost a nys after chanys. Either way the sense is 'since I do not know'. Arglwydes 'Lady'. medwl yw genhyf 'a mind is with me' = I intend. genhyf is gan 'with', 1 sg. y diuetha 'its destroying', to destroy it.

sentences.t: “A gwna ditheu yn llawen,” heb hi.
sentences.l: “And do you-for-your-part gladly,” said she.
sentences.i: “Then do so, and gladly,” she said.
sentences.n: yn llawen 'gladly': yn with an adjective makes an adverb. ll stays unsoftened after this yn (ll and rh resist it).

sentences.t: Ac yna y kyrchwys ef Orssed Arberth, a'r llygoden gantaw, a sengi dwy forch yn y lle uchaf ar yr orssed.
sentences.l: And then made-for he the Mound of-Arberth, and the mouse with-him, and treading-in two forks in the highest place on the mound.
sentences.i: And then he made for the Mound of Arberth with the mouse, and set up two forked posts on the highest point of the mound.
sentences.n: Ac yna y kyrchwys ef: after the opening adverb yna, the particle y and then the verb. kyrchwys, 3 sg. preterite in -wys of kyrchu 'make for'. Orssed Arberth 'the Mound of Arberth' (as in the First Branch) ← Gorssed, softened as the object following the subject ef. a'r llygoden gantaw 'and the mouse with him': gantaw is gan, 3 sg. masc. a sengi 'and treading', driving the posts into the ground. dwy forch 'two forks': forch is fforch with f written for ff, and ff has no soft mutation, so nothing shows after dwy. yr orssed ← gorssed, softened after the article (feminine).

sentences.t: Ac ual y byd yuelly, llyma y guelei yscolheic yn dyuot attaw, a hen dillat hydreul, tlawt amdanaw.
sentences.l: And as he-is thus, behold he-saw a-scholar coming to-him, and old clothes worn-out, poor about-him.
sentences.i: And as he was so engaged, he saw a scholar coming towards him, in old, threadbare, poor clothes.
sentences.n: ual y byd 'as he is': the vivid present of bot in a past narrative. yuelly 'thus'. llyma y guelei 'behold, he saw': here llyma is followed by y and a verb. guelei is the 3 sg. imperfect of gwelet (gu = gw). yscolheic 'scholar, clerk' (from Latin scholasticus), a man with some learning, often a poor wandering one. attaw 'to him' (at, 3 sg. masc.). a hen dillat 'and old clothes' ← dillat: hen stands before its noun and softens it. hydreul 'worn out' (hy- + treul 'wear', softened in the compound). amdanaw 'about him' (am, 3 sg. masc.).

sentences.t: Ac neut oed seith mlyned kyn no hynny, yr pan welsei ef na dyn, na mil, eithyr y pedwardyn y buassynt y gyt, yny golles y deu.
sentences.l: And lo it-was seven years before that, since he-had-seen neither man nor beast, except the four-persons that had-been together, until he-lost the two.
sentences.i: Now for seven years before then he had seen neither man nor beast, save the four who had been together until he lost two of them.
sentences.n: neut 'lo, indeed', the affirmative particle neu in the form it takes before a vowel. seith mlyned 'seven years' ← blyned: seith gives the nasal mutation to this word. kyn no hynny 'before that'. yr pan 'since (the time) when'. welsei ← gwelsei, 3 sg. pluperfect, softened after pan. na dyn, na mil 'neither man nor beast': mil 'animal'. eithyr 'except'. y pedwardyn 'the four persons', pedwar + dyn in one word. y buassynt 'had been', 3 pl. pluperfect of bot. y gyt 'together'. yny golles 'until he lost' ← colles, 3 sg. preterite of colli, softened after yny. y deu 'the two': Pryderi and Rhiannon, lost in the last part.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb yr yscolheic, “dyd da it.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said the scholar, “good day to-you.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said the scholar, “good day to you.”
sentences.n: dyd da it 'good day to you', the greeting of the First Branch. it 'to you', y conjugated (2 sg.).

sentences.t: “Duw a rodo da it, a grayssaw wrthyt,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “God may-he-give good to-you, and welcome towards-you,” said he.
sentences.i: “God give you good, and welcome to you,” he said.
sentences.n: Duw a rodo da it 'may God give you good': rodo is the present subjunctive of rodi, the mood of wishing, as in Duw a dalo. grayssaw 'welcome' (modern croeso) is the word's own form, not a mutation. wrthyt 'towards you' (wrth, 2 sg.).

sentences.t: “Pan doy di, yr yscolheic?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Whence come you, the scholar?” said he.
sentences.i: “Where do you come from, scholar?” he said.
sentences.n: Pan doy di 'whence do you come?': pan 'from where', doy 2 sg. present of dyuot, as in the First Branch. yr yscolheic: the noun in address takes the article, 'you, scholar'.

sentences.t: “Pan doaf, Arglwyd, o Loygyr o ganu. A phaham y gouynhy di, Arglwyd?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Whence I-come, Lord, from England from singing. And why do-you-ask you, Lord?” said he.
sentences.i: “I come, Lord, from England, where I have been singing. And why do you ask, Lord?” he said.
sentences.n: Pan doaf 'whence I come': he answers by taking up the words of the question. doaf is 1 sg. present of dyuot. o Loygyr 'from England' ← Lloygyr, softened after o (as in 008). o ganu 'from singing' ← kanu, softened after o: a poor scholar earned his keep by singing. A phaham 'and why' ← paham, spirant after a. y gouynhy 'do you ask', 2 sg. present of gouyn.

sentences.t: “Na weleis,” heb ef, “neut seith mlyned, un dyn yma, onyt pedwar dyn diholedic, a thitheu yr awr honn.”
sentences.l: “I-have-not-seen,” said he, “lo seven years, one man here, except four persons banished, and you-for-your-part this hour.”
sentences.i: “Because I have not seen a single man here,” he said, “these seven years, except four outcasts, and you yourself now.”
sentences.n: Na weleis 'I did not see' ← gweleis, 1 sg. preterite of gwelet, softened after na. The negative is na, not ny, because the sentence answers 'why?' as if it were a dependent clause: '(it is) that I have not seen'. The Red Book makes this explicit: am na weleis 'because I have not seen'. neut seith mlyned 'lo, seven years', as in 13. un dyn 'one man', a single person. onyt 'except'. diholedic 'banished, outcast' (deol 'exile'). a thitheu ← titheu, spirant after a. yr awr honn 'this hour', now.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd, mynet,” heb ef, “drwy y wlat honn yd wyf inheu yr awr honn, parth a'm gwlat uy hun. A pha ryw weith yd wyte yndaw, Arglwyd?”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord, going,” said he, “through this land I-am I-for-my-part this hour, towards my land my self. And what kind of work are-you in-it, Lord?”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” he said, “I am only passing through this land now, on my way to my own country. And what work is this you are about, Lord?”
sentences.n: In the manuscript a mark like '!' stands between Arglwyd and mynet. It is a mark, not a letter, as in 005 and 007, and nothing is missing (the Red Book has 'Je argl6yd heb ef mynet'). It is not printed. mynet … yd wyf 'going … I am': the verbal noun is put first, then yd wyf. y wlat honn 'this land' ← gwlat, softened after the article (feminine). parth a'm gwlat uy hun 'towards my own land': parth a 'towards'; 'm 'my' does not mutate gwlat. uy hun 'myself'. pha ryw weith ← gweith 'work', softened after ryw; pha has the spirant after a. yd wyte 'you are': wyt + te, the affixed pronoun 'you'. yndaw 'in it' (yn, 3 sg. masc.).

sentences.t: “Crogi lleidyr a geueis yn lledratta arnaf,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Hanging a-thief that I-got stealing on-me,” said he.
sentences.i: “Hanging a thief I caught stealing from me,” he said.
sentences.n: Crogi 'hanging': the answer to 'what work?' is the verbal noun alone. a geueis yn lledratta arnaf, as in 2.

sentences.t: “Ba ryw leidyr, Arglwyd?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What kind-of thief, Lord?” said he.
sentences.i: “What kind of thief, Lord?” he said.
sentences.n: Ba is a form of pa 'what', written with b; the scribe has Pa in the same question at 3 and 35. ryw leidyr ← lleidyr, softened after ryw.

sentences.t: “Pryf a welaf i'th law di ual llygoden. A drwc y gueda y wr kyuurd a thidi ymodi pryf kyfryw a hwnnw. Gellwg e ymdeith ef.”
sentences.l: “A-creature I-see in-your hand like a-mouse. And badly it-suits to a-man of-equal-rank with you-yourself to-handle a-creature such as that. Let-go away it.”
sentences.i: “I see a creature in your hand like a mouse. And it ill becomes a man of your rank to be handling a creature of that kind. Let it go.”
sentences.n: Pryf a welaf 'a creature I see': the object first. i'th law 'in your hand' ← llaw, softened after 'th; i is y = yn 'in'. ual llygoden 'like a mouse'. drwc y gueda 'badly it befits': drwc comes first, then y; gueda is 3 sg. present of gwedu (modern gweddu). y wr ← gwr, softened after y 'to'. ymodi: so in Evans and the second witness, here and at 37; the Red Book has teimlaw 'touch, handle' here, the word the White Book itself uses in 28. ymodi is properly 'stir, move'; here it must mean 'handle, busy oneself with', and that meaning comes from the context and the Red Book. kyfryw a hwnnw 'such as that'. Gellwg 'let go', 2 sg. imperative, written without the n of gellwng. e ymdeith 'away'.

sentences.t: “Na ellynghaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ynteu.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God,” said he-for-his-part.
sentences.i: “I will not let it go, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: Na ellynghaf 'I will not let go' ← gellynghaf, 1 sg. present of gellwng, softened after na, the negative used in answers. y rof a Duw 'between me and God' (house): rof is rwng 'between', 1 sg.

sentences.t: “Yn lledratta y keueis ef, a chyfreith lleidyr a wnaf inheu ac ef, y grogi.”
sentences.l: “Stealing I-got him, and the law of-a-thief I-will-do I-for-my-part with him: his hanging.”
sentences.i: “I caught him stealing, and I shall deal with him by the law for a thief: I shall hang him.”
sentences.n: Yn lledratta is put first, then the particle y: y keueis 'I caught', radical after y. ef 'him': the thief, and pryf is masculine. a chyfreith ← kyfreith 'law', spirant after a. a wnaf 'I will do', the abnormal order with the object first. ac ef 'with him'. y grogi 'his hanging' ← krogi, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ynteu, “rac guelet gwr kyuurd a thidi yn y gueith hwnnw, punt a geueis i o gardotta, mi a'e rodaf it, a gellwng y pryf hwnnw e ymdeith.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he-for-his-part, “against seeing a-man of-equal-rank with you-yourself in that work, a-pound that I-got from begging, I it-is-that will-give-it to-you, and let-go that creature away.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “rather than see a man of your rank at such work, I will give you a pound that I got by begging; and you let that creature go.”
sentences.n: In the manuscript the same '!' mark as in 19 stands between rac and guelet. It is a mark, nothing is missing, and it is not printed. rac guelet 'against seeing', to avoid seeing. yn y gueith hwnnw 'in that work'. punt 'a pound' is put first and then taken up by 'e in mi a'e rodaf 'I will give it'. o gardotta 'by begging' ← kardotta, softened after o. a gellwng 'and let go', the imperative.

sentences.t: “Nac ellynghaf, y rof a Duw, nys guerthaf.”
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God, I-will-not-sell-it.”
sentences.i: “I will not let it go, between me and God, nor will I sell it.”
sentences.n: Nac ellynghaf: nac is na before a vowel. nys guerthaf 'I will not sell it': ny + the infixed 's 'it'. guerthaf, 1 sg. present of gwerthu, is radical after nys.

sentences.t: “Gwna di, Arglwyd,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Do you, Lord,” said he.
sentences.i: “Have it your way, Lord,” he said.
sentences.n: Gwna di 'do (so), you': the imperative, with di ← ti softened after the verb.

sentences.t: “Ony bei hagyr guelet gwr kyuurd a thidi yn teimlaw y ryw bryf a hwnnw, ny'm torei.”
sentences.l: “Unless it-were ugly seeing a-man of-equal-rank with you-yourself handling that kind of creature, it-would-not-trouble-me.”
sentences.i: “Were it not unsightly to see a man of your rank handling a creature of that kind, it would be nothing to me.”
sentences.n: Ony bei 'if it were not'. hagyr 'ugly, unsightly'. yn teimlaw 'handling, touching', the word the Red Book has in 22. y ryw bryf a hwnnw 'that kind of creature' (pryf softened after ryw). ny'm torei 'it would not trouble me': 'm 'me' is infixed after ny; torei is 3 sg. imperfect of torri, used in the sense 'matter to, concern'.

sentences.t: Ac e ymdeith yd aeth yr yscolheic.
sentences.l: And away went the scholar.
sentences.i: And the scholar went on his way.
sentences.n: e ymdeith 'away' is put first, then yd aeth 'went' (3 sg. preterite of mynet). In the manuscript the h of yscolheic is written above the line, between l and eic; it is brought into the line.

sentences.t: Val y byd ynteu yn dodi y dulath yn y fyrch, nachaf offeirat yn dyuot ataw, ar uarch yn gyweir.
sentences.l: As he-is he-for-his-part putting the crossbeam in the forks, behold a-priest coming to-him, on a-horse equipped.
sentences.i: As he was setting the crossbeam in the forks, a priest came towards him on a horse in full harness.
sentences.n: Val y byd ynteu 'as he is', the vivid present again. dulath 'crossbeam', the bar laid across the forks. yn y fyrch 'in the forks': ffyrch is the plural of fforch, written with f for ff. nachaf 'behold', which does not soften (offeirat). ataw 'to him', written with one t here. ar uarch ← march, softened after ar. yn gyweir 'equipped, harnessed' ← kyweir, softened after yn.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd, dyd da it,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Lord, good day to-you,” said he.
sentences.i: “Lord, good day to you,” he said.
sentences.n: The scholar's greeting, word for word.

sentences.t: “Duw a ro da it,” heb y Manawydan, “a'th uendith.”
sentences.l: “God may-he-give good to-you,” said Manawydan, “and your blessing.”
sentences.i: “God give you good,” said Manawydan, “and your blessing.”
sentences.n: ro is a shorter form of rodo, the present subjunctive of wishing. heb y Manawydan. a'th uendith 'and your blessing' ← bendith, softened after 'th. To a priest he adds a request for his blessing.

sentences.t: “Bendith Duw it. A pha ryw weith, Arglwyd, yd wyd yn y wneuthur?”
sentences.l: “The-blessing of-God to-you. And what kind of work, Lord, are-you in its doing?”
sentences.i: “God's blessing on you. And what work is this you are doing, Lord?”
sentences.n: Bendith Duw it 'God's blessing to you'. yd wyd 'you are'. yn y wneuthur 'in its doing' ← gwneuthur, softened after y 'its' (it refers to gweith, masculine).

sentences.t: “Crogi lleidyr a geueis yn lledratta arnaf,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Hanging a-thief that I-got stealing on-me,” said he.
sentences.i: “Hanging a thief I caught stealing from me,” he said.
sentences.n: The same answer as he gave the scholar (20).

sentences.t: “Pa ryw leidyr, Arglwyd?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What kind-of thief, Lord?” said he.
sentences.i: “What kind of thief, Lord?” he said.
sentences.n: Pa ryw leidyr, as in 3.

sentences.t: “Pryf,” heb ynteu, “ar ansawd llygoden, a lledratta a wnaeth arnaf, a dihenyd lleidyr a wnaf inheu arnaw ef.”
sentences.l: “A-creature,” said he-for-his-part, “in the appearance of-a-mouse, and stealing it-did on-me, and the death of-a-thief I-will-do I-for-my-part on-him.”
sentences.i: “A creature with the appearance of a mouse,” he said, “and it has been stealing from me, and I shall put it to a thief's death.”
sentences.n: ar ansawd llygoden 'in the appearance of a mouse': ansawd 'appearance' (house). lledratta a wnaeth 'stealing it did', the verbal noun with a wnaeth. dihenyd 'death, execution'. arnaw ef 'on him' (ar, 3 sg. masc.).

sentences.t: “Arglwyd, rac dy welet yn ymodi y pryf hwnnw, mi a'y prynaf. Ellwng ef.”
sentences.l: “Lord, against your seeing handling that creature, I it-is-that will-buy-it. Let-go it.”
sentences.i: “Lord, rather than see you handling that creature, I will buy it. Let it go.”
sentences.n: rac dy welet 'against seeing you': dy is the object of the verbal noun, which is softened after it (gwelet). yn ymodi 'handling', the word of 22 again. The Red Book has teimlaw here too, as in 22, so ymodi in both places is the White Book's own word. mi a'y prynaf 'I will buy it': 'y is the infixed object. Ellwng 'let go': the imperative of ellwng, a form of gellwng without the g (as in the First Branch).

sentences.t: “Y Duw y dygaf uyghyffes, na'y werthu, na'y ollwng nas gwnaf i.”
sentences.l: “To God I-bear my-confession, neither its selling nor its letting-go, I-will-not-do-it I.”
sentences.i: “I pledge my faith to God, I will neither sell it nor let it go.”
sentences.n: Y Duw y dygaf uyghyffes 'to God I bear my confession', an oath. dygaf is 1 sg. present of dwyn. uyghyffes is uy 'my' + kyffes with the nasal mutation, written gh for ngh (contrast ym kyffes in 5). na'y werthu, na'y ollwng 'neither its selling nor its loosing': na 'nor' + 'y 'its', which softens gwerthu and gollwng. nas gwnaf i 'I will not do it': na + 's 'it'.

sentences.t: “Guir yw, Arglwyd, nyt guerth arnaw ef dim. Rac dy welet ti yn ymhalogi wrth y pryf hwnnw, mi a rodaf it deir punt, a gollwng ef e ymdeith.”
sentences.l: “True it-is, Lord, there-is-not a-price on-it anything. Against your seeing you defiling-yourself with that creature, I it-is-that will-give to-you three pounds, and let-go it away.”
sentences.i: “True it is, Lord, it is worth nothing. But rather than see you defile yourself with that creature, I will give you three pounds; and you let it go.”
sentences.n: nyt guerth arnaw ef dim 'there is no price on it at all'. ymhalogi 'defile oneself' (ym- + halogi). deir punt 'three pounds' ← teir, the feminine numeral, softened: the object of the verb, with it 'to you' standing between. The Red Book has teirpunt unsoftened, and pedeirpunt in 55 is unsoftened in the same position here, so the rule is not applied every time. gollwng is the imperative (a form of gellwng).

sentences.t: “Na uynhaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ynteu, “un guerth, namyn yr hwnn a dyly, y grogi.”
sentences.l: “I-do-not-want, between me and God,” said he-for-his-part, “any price, but that-which it-deserves: its hanging.”
sentences.i: “I want no price, between me and God,” he said, “but what it deserves: to hang.”
sentences.n: Na uynhaf 'I do not want' ← mynhaf, 1 sg. present of mynnu, softened after na. un guerth 'one price', any price. yr hwnn a dyly 'that which it deserves': dyly is 3 sg. present of dylyu. y grogi 'its hanging'.

sentences.t: “En llawen, Arglwyd, gwna dy uympwy.”
sentences.l: “Gladly, Lord, do your pleasure.”
sentences.i: “Gladly, Lord: do as you please.”
sentences.n: En llawen 'gladly' is yn llawen, written with e for y, as in e ymdeith. So in Evans. dy uympwy 'your whim, your pleasure' ← mympwy, softened after dy.

sentences.t: E ymdeith yd aeth yr offeirat.
sentences.l: Away went the priest.
sentences.i: The priest went on his way.
sentences.n: E ymdeith yd aeth, as with the scholar (29).

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth ynteu, maglu y llinin am uynwgyl y llygoden.
sentences.l: That-is what did he-for-his-part: noosing the string about the neck of the mouse.
sentences.i: Then he knotted the string round the mouse's neck.
sentences.n: Sef a wnaeth ynteu 'that is what he did', answered by a verbal noun: maglu 'snare, noose'. llinin 'string, cord'. am uynwgyl ← mynwgyl 'neck', softened after am. y llygoden: llygoden is feminine, but ll does not soften after the article.

sentences.t: Ac ual yd oed yn y dyrchauael, llyma rwtter escob a welei a'y swmereu a'y yniuer; a'r escop e hun yn kyrchu parth ac attaw.
sentences.l: And as he-was in its raising, behold the-train of-a-bishop that he-saw, and his packs and his company; and the bishop himself making-for towards to-him.
sentences.i: And as he was hoisting it up, he saw a bishop's train, with his packs and his company, and the bishop himself making his way towards him.
sentences.n: ual yd oed 'as he was'. yn y dyrchauael 'in its raising', raising it up (dyrchafael). llyma rwtter escob a welei 'behold, a bishop's train he saw': the object first, after llyma. rwtter 'train, retinue' looks like a borrowing (compare English rout 'company'); its form is not certain. swmereu 'packs, sumpter-loads', plural of swmer (57). a'y yniuer 'and his company'. e hun 'himself'. parth ac attaw 'towards him': parth a 'towards', with ac before the vowel.

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth ynteu, gohir ar y weith.
sentences.l: That-is what did he-for-his-part: delaying on his work.
sentences.i: He held off from his work.
sentences.n: Sef a wnaeth ynteu, gohir 'that is what he did: delaying'. gohir is the verbal noun 'put off, delay'. ar y weith ← gweith, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd escop,” heb ef, “dy uendith.”
sentences.l: “Lord bishop,” said he, “your blessing.”
sentences.i: “Lord Bishop,” he said, “your blessing.”
sentences.n: Arglwyd escop 'Lord Bishop', the address. dy uendith ← bendith, softened after dy.

sentences.t: “Duw a rodo y uendith it,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “God may-he-give his blessing to-you,” said he.
sentences.i: “God give you his blessing,” he said.
sentences.n: Duw a rodo, the subjunctive of wishing. In the manuscript the y before uendith is written above the line; it is brought into the line. y uendith 'his blessing' ← bendith, softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “Pa ryw weith yd wyt ty yndaw?”
sentences.l: “What kind of work are-you you in-it?”
sentences.i: “What work is this you are about?”
sentences.n: yd wyt ty 'you are, you': ty is ti. yndaw 'in it'.

sentences.t: “Crogi lleidyr a geueis yn lledratta arnaf,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Hanging a-thief that I-got stealing on-me,” said he.
sentences.i: “Hanging a thief I caught stealing from me,” he said.
sentences.n: The same answer, the third time.

sentences.t: “Ponyt llygoden,” heb ynteu, “a welaf i y'th law di?”
sentences.l: “Is-it-not a-mouse,” said he-for-his-part, “that I-see in your hand you?”
sentences.i: “Is it not a mouse,” he said, “that I see in your hand?”
sentences.n: Ponyt 'is it not?', a question expecting yes. a welaf i 'that I see'. y'th law 'in your hand': y for yn before 'th, which softens llaw.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “a lleidyr uu hi arnaf i.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “and a-thief was she on-me I.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “and she has been a thief to me.”
sentences.n: lleidyr uu hi 'a thief she was': lleidyr is put first, and uu ← bu is softened as after the relative a, which is not written here. hi 'she': the mouse, llygoden being feminine. arnaf i 'on me'.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “can doethwyf i ar diuetha y pryf hwnnw, mi a'y prynaf y genhyt.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “since I-have-come upon the destroying of that creature, I it-is-that will-buy-it from-you.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “since I have come upon the destruction of that creature, I will buy it from you.
sentences.n: can 'since'. doethwyf 'I have come': so Evans and the second witness; the Red Book has deuthum 'I came', the ordinary 1 sg. preterite. doethwyf is built on the stem doeth- with the 1 sg. ending -wyf, used here as a perfect; its exact analysis is not certain. ar diuetha 'upon the destroying'. mi a'y prynaf 'I will buy it': Evans prints aý (the y is certain on the image), where the second witness has a'e. The infixed pronoun refers to the mouse (llygoden, feminine), and 'y is the White Book's usual spelling for 'her, it'. y genhyt 'from you' (y gan, 2 sg.). The English says 'it' because the bishop goes on to speak of the creature as masculine (yrdaw, gollwng ef).

sentences.t: Mi a rodaf seith punt it yrdaw, a rac guelet gwr kyuurd a thi yn diuetha pryf mor dielw a hwnnw, gollwng ef, a'r da a geffy ditheu.”
sentences.l: I it-is-that will-give seven pounds to-you for-it, and against seeing a-man of-equal-rank with you destroying a-creature as worthless as that, let-go it, and the goods you-will-get you-for-your-part.”
sentences.i: I will give you seven pounds for it; and rather than see a man of your rank destroying so worthless a creature, let it go, and the money is yours.”
sentences.n: seith punt 'seven pounds': punt is not nasalised after seith (only a few words, like blyned, mlyned, in 13, are). yrdaw 'for it', er conjugated (3 sg. masc.; compare yrdhunt in the last part). a thi 'with you', the plain pronoun this time. mor dielw a hwnnw 'as worthless as that': mor + adjective + a; dielw is di- + elw 'profit'. a'r da 'and the goods', the money. a geffy 'you will get' ← keffy, 2 sg. present of kaffael, softened after a.

sentences.t: “Na ellynghaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ynteu.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God,” said he-for-his-part.
sentences.i: “I will not let it go, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: Na ellynghaf, y rof a Duw, as in 23.

sentences.t: “Kanys gollyngy yr hynny, mi a rodaf it pedeirpunt ar ugeint o aryant parawt, a gellwng ef.”
sentences.l: “Since you-will-not-let-go-it for that, I it-is-that will-give to-you four-pounds on twenty of silver ready, and let-go it.”
sentences.i: “Since you will not let it go for that, I will give you twenty-four pounds in ready silver; and let it go.”
sentences.n: Kanys gollyngy 'since you will not let it go': as in 9, Kanys must be kan 'since' + nys 'not … it', since the bishop is raising his offer, and the Red Book writes it out as two words, Kan nys gollynghy. gollyngy is 2 sg. present of gollwng (gellwng), radical after nys. yr hynny 'for that' (yr = er). pedeirpunt ar ugeint 'four pounds on twenty' = twenty-four (Welsh counts by twenties); pedeir is the feminine of pedwar. It stands unsoftened here although it 'to you' comes between, whereas deir punt in 39 is softened. The mutation is not applied every time. o aryant parawt 'of ready silver', in coin.

sentences.t: “Na ellynghaf, dygaf y Duw uyghyffes, yr y gymeint arall,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, I-bear to God my-confession, for its as-much other,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will not let it go, I pledge my faith to God, not for as much again,” he said.
sentences.n: dygaf y Duw uyghyffes, the oath of 38 in a different order. yr y gymeint arall 'for its as-much again': kymeint 'as much', softened after y 'its'; that is, double the sum.

sentences.t: “Canys collyghy yr hynny,” heb ef, “mi a rodaf it a wely o uarch yn y maes hwnn, a seith swmer yssyd yma, ar y seith meirch y maent arnunt.”
sentences.l: “Since you-will-not-let-go-it for that,” said he, “I it-is-that will-give to-you what you-see of horse in this field, and the seven packs that-are here, on the seven horses that they-are on-them.”
sentences.i: “Since you will not let it go for that,” he said, “I will give you every horse you see in this field, and the seven packs that are here, on the seven horses that carry them.”
sentences.n: Canys collyghy is the Kanys gollyngy of 55 written differently: c for g and gh for ngh. It is a spelling, not a mutation. The Red Book has Kan nys gellyngy here. a wely 'what you see' ← gwely, 2 sg. present of gwelet, softened after a. o uarch 'of horse' ← march, softened after o. seith swmer 'seven packs, loads'. ar y seith meirch y maent arnunt 'on the seven horses that they are on': arnunt 'on them' (ar, 3 pl.) completes the relative clause, 'on which they are'. Evans prints ar ýſeith in one, divided ar y seith as in the second witness.

sentences.t: “Na uynhaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ynteu.
sentences.l: “I-do-not-want, between me and God,” said he-for-his-part.
sentences.i: “I do not want that, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: Na uynhaf, as in 40.

sentences.t: “Cany mynny hynny, gwna y guerth.”
sentences.l: “Since-not you-want that, make the price.”
sentences.i: “Since you will not take that, name your price.”
sentences.n: Cany 'since … not' (kan + ny). mynny is 2 sg. present of mynnu, written unsoftened after ny. The White Book writes m both ways after ny: ny mynneis (002), ny mynnwys (004), but ny uynhei (007); the Red Book also has cany mynny here. gwna y guerth 'make the price': y is the article, and gwerth is masculine, so it is not softened.

sentences.t: “Gwnaf,” heb ynteu, “rydhau Riannon a Phryderi.”
sentences.l: “I-will-do,” said he-for-his-part, “freeing Rhiannon and Pryderi.”
sentences.i: “I will,” he said: “the freeing of Rhiannon and Pryderi.”
sentences.n: Gwnaf 'I will do': he says yes by repeating the verb. rydhau 'set free' (rhyddhau; r for rh). a Phryderi ← Pryderi, spirant after a.

sentences.t: “Ti a gehy hynny.”
sentences.l: “You it-is-that will-get that.”
sentences.i: “You shall have that.”
sentences.n: Ti a gehy 'you will get': so Evans, once only; the same promise is a geffy in 65 and 80. Both are taken as 2 sg. present of kaffael, softened after a ('you will get'); gehy is best taken as a by-form of gey (compare a gey in the last part): the Red Book has Ti a gey here, so it is not a slip for geffy. The sense is not in doubt.

sentences.t: “Na uynhaf, y rof a Duw.”
sentences.l: “I-do-not-want, between me and God.”
sentences.i: “I do not want that, between me and God.”
sentences.n: Manawydan refuses even this, to get the rest.

sentences.t: “Beth a uynhy ditheu?”
sentences.l: “What do-you-want you-for-your-part?”
sentences.i: “What do you want, then?”
sentences.n: Beth ← peth 'what'. a uynhy 'do you want' ← mynhy, 2 sg. present of mynnu, softened after a. ditheu ← titheu.

sentences.t: “Guaret yr hut a'r lledrith y ar seith cantref Dyuet.”
sentences.l: “Removing the enchantment and the illusion from-off the seven cantrefs of-Dyfed.”
sentences.i: “The lifting of the enchantment and the illusion from the seven cantrefs of Dyfed.”
sentences.n: Guaret 'removing' (gwaret, as in the First Branch). hut 'enchantment, magic' (as in the last part). lledrith 'illusion, magic, phantasm': here written with d, but lletrith with t at 75. Both are as in Evans; the Red Book has lletrith in both places. y ar 'from off' (y 'from' + ar 'on').

sentences.t: “Ti a geffy hynny heuyt, a gellwng y llygoden.”
sentences.l: “You it-is-that will-get that also, and let-go the mouse.”
sentences.i: “You shall have that too; and let the mouse go.”
sentences.n: a geffy 'you will get', the usual form (compare gehy in 61). heuyt 'also'. gellwng, imperative.

sentences.t: “Na ellyngaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will not let it go, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: Na ellyngaf, here spelt without h (ellynghaf elsewhere).

sentences.t: “Gwybot a uynhaf pwy yw y llygoden.”
sentences.l: “Knowing it-is-that I-want who is the mouse.”
sentences.i: “I want to know who the mouse is.”
sentences.n: Gwybot 'knowing' is put first as the object of a uynhaf 'I want' (mynhaf, softened after a). pwy yw 'who is'.

sentences.t: “Wy gwreic i yw hi, a phy ny bei hynny nys dillyngwn.”
sentences.l: “My wife I is she, and if-not were that, I-would-not-release-her.”
sentences.i: “She is my wife; and were it not for that, I would not be seeking her release.”
sentences.n: Wy gwreic i 'my wife': wy stands for uy 'my'. The part writes 'my wife' three ways, all kept as in Evans: wy gwreic here and in 87, uy gwreic in 74, uy ngwreic, with the nasal mutation written, in 92. a phy ny bei 'and if it were not': py is pei 'if', with the spirant after a; bei is the imperfect subjunctive of bot. nys dillyngwn 'I would not release her': ny + 's 'her'; dillyngwn is 1 sg. imperfect of dillwng, another form of gellwng.

sentences.t: “Pa gyffuryf y doeth hi attaf i?”
sentences.l: “What manner that she-came to-me I?”
sentences.i: “How did she come to me?”
sentences.n: Pa gyffuryf 'in what manner' ← kyffuryf 'form, manner', softened after pa. y doeth hi 'she came'. attaf i 'to me' (at, 1 sg.).

sentences.t: “Y herwa,” heb ynteu.
sentences.l: “To raid,” said he-for-his-part.
sentences.i: “On a raid,” he said.
sentences.n: Y herwa 'to go raiding': herwa 'raid, plunder, live as an outlaw' (from herw 'outlawry'), with y 'to'. The word division is the second witness's.

sentences.t: “Miui yw Llwyt uab Kil Coet, a mi a dodeis yr hut ar seith cantref Dyuet, ac y dial Guawl uab Clut, o gedymdeithas ac ef y dodeis i yr hut;
sentences.l: “I-myself am Llwyd son of-Cil Coed, and I it-is-that put the enchantment on the seven cantrefs of-Dyfed, and to avenge Gwawl son of-Clud, out-of fellowship with him, I-put I the enchantment;
sentences.i: “I am Llwyd son of Cil Coed, and it was I who put the enchantment on the seven cantrefs of Dyfed; and it was to avenge Gwawl son of Clud, out of fellowship with him, that I put the enchantment on;
sentences.n: Miui 'I myself', the doubled pronoun (mi + ui ← mi). Llwyt uab Kil Coet is Llwyd son of Cil Coed: uab ← mab, softened after a name, and final -t = -d. a mi a dodeis 'and I put': dodeis, 1 sg. preterite of dodi. ac y dial … y dodeis i 'and to avenge … I put': the purpose phrase is put first, then the particle y and the verb. Guawl uab Clut is Gwawl son of Clud, the suitor Pwyll caught in the bag in the First Branch. o gedymdeithas ← kedymdeithas 'fellowship' (house), softened after o.

sentences.t: ac ar Pryderi y dieleis i guare broch yghot a Guawl uab Clut, pan y gwnaeth Pwyll Penn Annwn; a hynny yn Llys Eueyd Hen y gwnaeth o aghynghor.
sentences.l: and on Pryderi I-avenged I the playing of badger in-a-bag with Gwawl son of-Clud, when Pwyll Head of-Annwfn did-it; and that in the Court of-Hefeydd the-Old he-did-it out-of ill-counsel.
sentences.i: and it was on Pryderi that I avenged the game of Badger in the Bag played on Gwawl son of Clud, when Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, played it; and that he did at the court of Hefeydd the Old, on ill counsel.
sentences.n: ar Pryderi y dieleis i 'on Pryderi I avenged': the phrase first, then y. dieleis is the 1 sg. preterite of dial. Its object guare stands unsoftened after the subject i (contrast Orssed after ef in 11); the Red Book has gware too. Pryderi stands unsoftened after ar, here and in 83. guare broch yghot 'the playing of badger in the bag' (the game in 003: broch yg got). yghot is yng nghot: yn 'in' + cot with the nasal mutation, written gh for ngh. a Guawl 'with Gwawl', meaning on him. pan y gwnaeth 'when he did it': y here is best taken as the infixed object 'it', the game. Pwyll Penn Annwn 'Pwyll, Head of Annwfn' (the spelling Annwn as in 003). Llys Eueyd Hen 'the court of Hefeydd the Old', Rhiannon's father (003). o aghynghor 'out of ill counsel': an- 'un-, ill' + kynghor, written agh- for angh-.

sentences.t: A guedy clybot dy uot yn kyuanhedu y wlat, y doeth uyn teulu attaf inheu, ac y erchi eu rithyaw yn llygot y diua dy yd, ac y doethant y nos gyntaf uyn teulu e hunein.
sentences.l: And after hearing your being inhabiting the land, came my household-troop to me for-my-part, and to ask their transforming into mice to destroy your corn, and they-came the first night, my household-troop themselves.
sentences.i: And when it was heard that you were settling the land, my warband came to me and asked to be changed into mice to destroy your corn; and on the first night it was my warband alone that came.
sentences.n: guedy clybot 'after hearing': clybot is a verbal noun of clywet. dy uot 'your being' ← bot, softened after dy. yn kyuanhedu 'inhabiting, settling'. uyn teulu 'my household-troop' (house: 'warband'): the nasal is written on the possessive, uyn for uy, while teulu itself is left unmutated (compare uym pryder in 004). ac y erchi 'and to ask': y 'to' + erchi. eu rithyaw 'their transforming' (rhithiaw 'give a shape to'; r for rh). yn llygot 'into mice': ll is not softened after yn. y diua 'to destroy'. dy yd 'your corn' (yt, here yd). y nos gyntaf 'the first night' ← kyntaf, softened after the feminine nos. e hunein 'themselves', by themselves.

sentences.t: A'r eil nos y doethant heuyt, ac y diuayssant y dwy grofd. A'r tryded nos y doeth uy gwreic a gwraged y llys attaf, y erchi im eu rithaw, ac y ritheis inheu. A beichawc oed hi.
sentences.l: And the second night they-came also, and they-destroyed the two crofts. And the third night came my wife and the women of the court to-me, to ask of-me their transforming, and I-transformed for-my-part. And pregnant was she.
sentences.i: On the second night they came too, and destroyed the two crofts. And on the third night my wife and the women of the court came to me and asked me to change them, and I changed them. And she was with child.
sentences.n: eil 'second'. y diuayssant 'they destroyed', 3 pl. preterite in -yssant of diua. y dwy grofd 'the two crofts': dwy softens, so grofd is regular here. A'r tryded nos 'and the third night': tryded is written unsoftened, though the article before a feminine noun's ordinal usually softens it (dryded). The Red Book also has A'r tryded nos. uy gwreic 'my wife': the nasal (ngwreic) is not written; compare 68. gwraged 'women', plural of gwreic. y erchi im 'to ask me'. eu rithaw, the same verb as rithyaw in 73, spelt without y. y ritheis inheu 'and I transformed (them)', 1 sg. preterite. beichawc 'pregnant' is put first, then oed.

sentences.t: A phy na bei ueichawc hi, nis gordiwedut ti. A chanys bu, a'y dala hi, mi a rodaf Pryderi a Riannon it, ac a waredaf yr hut a'r lletrith y ar Dyuet.
sentences.l: And if-not were pregnant she, you-would-not-overtake-her you. And since it-was, and her catching, I it-is-that will-give Pryderi and Rhiannon to-you, and will-remove the enchantment and the illusion from-off Dyfed.
sentences.i: And had she not been with child, you would never have caught her. But since she was, and has been caught, I will give you Pryderi and Rhiannon, and lift the enchantment and the illusion from Dyfed.
sentences.n: A phy na bei 'and if (she) were not': py 'if' with na, as with ny in 68. ueichawc ← beichawc, softened as the predicate after bei. nis gordiwedut 'you would not have overtaken her': ni + 's 'her'; gordiwedut is a 2 sg. imperfect of gordiwes 'overtake'. A chanys bu 'and since (she) was': here canys is plain 'since', affirmative (compare 9 and 55). a'y dala hi 'and her catching': 'y 'her' as the object of the verbal noun. ac a waredaf 'and I will remove' ← gwaredaf, softened after a. lletrith: here written with t (lledrith in 64); both as Evans.

sentences.t: Minheu a uenegeis yti pwy yw hi, a gellwng hi.”
sentences.l: I-for-my-part it-is-that have-told to-you who is she, and let-go her.”
sentences.i: I have told you who she is: now let her go.”
sentences.n: Minheu 'I for my part'. a uenegeis 'have told' ← menegeis, 1 sg. preterite of menegi, softened after a. yti 'to you', a fuller form of it.

sentences.t: “Na ellynghaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will not let her go, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: Na ellynghaf, as before.

sentences.t: “Beth a uynny ditheu?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What do-you-want you-for-your-part?” said he.
sentences.i: “What do you want, then?” he said.
sentences.n: a uynny ← mynny, 2 sg. present of mynnu, softened after a (written uynhy in 63).

sentences.t: “Llyna,” heb ynteu, “a uynhaf, na bo hut uyth ar seith cantref Dyuet, ac na dotter.”
sentences.l: “There-is,” said he-for-his-part, “what I-want: that there-be-not enchantment ever on the seven cantrefs of-Dyfed, and that it-be-not-put.”
sentences.i: “This is what I want,” he said: “that there be no enchantment ever on the seven cantrefs of Dyfed, and that none be put on them.”
sentences.n: Llyna … a uynhaf 'there is what I want'. na bo 'that there be not': bo is the 3 sg. present subjunctive of bot. uyth 'ever' ← byth, softened as an adverb. na dotter 'that (it) be not put': dotter is the impersonal present subjunctive of dodi (as a dotter in 003).

sentences.t: “Ti a geffy hynny,” heb ef, “a gellwng hi.”
sentences.l: “You it-is-that will-get that,” said he, “and let-go her.”
sentences.i: “You shall have that,” he said, “and let her go.”
sentences.n: a geffy, as in 65.

sentences.t: “Na ellynghaf, y rof a Duw,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-not-let-go, between me and God,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will not let her go, between me and God,” he said.
sentences.n: The refusal once more.

sentences.t: “Beth a uynny ditheu?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What do-you-want you-for-your-part?” said he.
sentences.i: “What do you want, then?” he said.
sentences.n: As in 78.

sentences.t: “Llyna,” heb ef, “a uynhaf, na bo ymdiala ar Pryderi a Riannon, nac arnaf inheu, uyth am hynn.”
sentences.l: “There-is,” said he, “what I-want: that there-be-not avenging on Pryderi and Rhiannon, nor on-me I-for-my-part, ever for this.”
sentences.i: “This is what I want,” he said: “that no vengeance ever be taken for this on Pryderi and Rhiannon, nor on me.”
sentences.n: ymdiala 'taking vengeance' (ym- + dial). ar Pryderi, unsoftened, as in 72. nac arnaf inheu 'nor on me': nac is na 'nor' before a vowel. am hynn 'for this'.

sentences.t: “Hynny oll a geffy. A dioer, da y medreist,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “That all you-will-get. And assuredly, well you-have-hit,” said he.
sentences.i: “All that you shall have. And indeed, you have hit the mark well,” he said.
sentences.n: Hynny oll a geffy 'all that you will get', the object first. Dioer 'assuredly' (house: i 'Indeed'). da y medreist 'well you hit': da is put first, then y. medreist is the 2 sg. preterite of medru 'hit (a mark), know how'.

sentences.t: “Bei na metrut hynny,” heb ef, “ef a doy am dy benn cwbyl o'r gouut.”
sentences.l: “If you-had-not-hit that,” said he, “it it-is-that would-come about your head the-whole of the grief.”
sentences.i: “Had you not hit on that,” he said, “the whole of the trouble would have come down upon your head.”
sentences.n: Bei na metrut 'if you had not hit': metrut is the 2 sg. imperfect subjunctive of medru, written with t, and left unsoftened after na. ef a doy 'it would come': ef is the empty subject 'it'. doy seems to stand for doei, the 3 sg. imperfect of dyuot, 'would come'; it is not the doy 'you come' of 16. The Red Book has ef a doei here, which confirms it. am dy benn 'about your head' ← penn, softened after dy. cwbyl 'the whole'. o'r gouut 'of the grief, trouble' (gofid).

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “rac hynny y nodeis inheu.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “against that I-stipulated I-for-my-part.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “it was against that I made my terms.”
sentences.n: rac hynny 'against that' is put first, then the particle y. nodeis 'I stipulated', 1 sg. preterite of nodi 'mark, specify'.

sentences.t: “A rytha weithon wy gwreic im.”
sentences.l: “And free now my wife for-me.”
sentences.i: “Now set my wife free for me.”
sentences.n: rytha 'free', 2 sg. imperative of rydhau (rhyddhau). weithon 'now'. wy gwreic, the spelling of 68. im 'for me'.

sentences.t: “Na rydhaaf, y rof a Duw, yny welwyf Pryderi a Riannon yn ryd gyt a mi.”
sentences.l: “I-will-not-free, between me and God, until I-see Pryderi and Rhiannon free together with me.”
sentences.i: “I will not, between me and God, until I see Pryderi and Rhiannon free beside me.”
sentences.n: Na rydhaaf 'I will not free', 1 sg. present of rydhau. yny welwyf 'until I see' ← gwelwyf, 1 sg. present subjunctive, softened after yny. yn ryd 'free' (rhydd). gyt a mi 'with me'.

sentences.t: “Wely di yma wynteu yn dyuot,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “See you here them-for-their-part coming,” said he.
sentences.i: “See, here they come,” he said.
sentences.n: Wely di 'you see' ← gwely, 2 sg. present, softened (as wely dy in 004). wynteu 'they for their part'. yn dyuot 'coming'.

sentences.t: Ar hynny, llyma Pryderi a Riannon.
sentences.l: At that, behold Pryderi and Rhiannon.
sentences.i: At that, there were Pryderi and Rhiannon.
sentences.n: Ar hynny 'at that, thereupon'. llyma 'behold'.

sentences.t: Kyuodi a oruc ynteu yn eu herbyn, a'y graessawu, ac eisted y gyt.
sentences.l: Rising he-did he-for-his-part to-meet-them, and their welcoming, and sitting together.
sentences.i: He rose to meet them, and welcomed them, and they sat down together.
sentences.n: Kyuodi a oruc ynteu 'rising he did'. yn eu herbyn 'to meet them': erbyn with h after eu 'their', before the vowel. a'y graessawu 'and their welcoming': 'y 'their' leaves a consonant unmutated, and graessawu, like grayssaw in 15, has g as its own initial. eisted y gyt 'sitting together'.

sentences.t: “A wrda, rytha uy ngwreic im weithon, ac neu ry geueist gwbyl o'r a nodeist.”
sentences.l: “O nobleman, free my wife for-me now, and lo you-have-got the-whole of what you-stipulated.”
sentences.i: “Nobleman, set my wife free for me now: you have had all that you stipulated.”
sentences.n: A wrda 'O nobleman' ← gwrda (gwr + da, the singular of gwyrda), softened after the vocative a. uy ngwreic 'my wife': here the nasal mutation is written. Evans has uyng6reic, as in the second witness; compare 68. neu ry geueist 'lo, you have got': neu is the affirmative particle, and ry, the perfective particle, softens keueist. gwbyl 'the whole' ← cwbyl, softened as the object directly after the verb, a softening Middle Welsh shows only sometimes. o'r a nodeist 'of what you stipulated' (nodeist, 2 sg. preterite).

sentences.t: “Ellynghaf yn llawen,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-release gladly,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will, gladly,” he said.
sentences.n: Ellynghaf 'I will release', from ellwng (gellwng without the g). He answers yes by repeating the verb.

sentences.t: Ac yna y gollwng hi, ac y trewis ynteu hi a hudlath, ac y datrithwys hi yn wreigyang geccaf a welsei neb.
sentences.l: And then he-releases her, and struck he-for-his-part her with a-magic-wand, and he-disenchanted her into the young-woman fairest that anyone had-seen.
sentences.i: And then Manawydan let her go, and Llwyd struck her with a magic wand and turned her back into the fairest young woman anyone had ever seen.
sentences.n: y gollwng hi 'he lets her go': gollwng here is the 3 sg. present (the bare stem), the vivid present; it is Manawydan who lets her go. The Red Book has the preterite instead, y gellyngawd ef hi 'he let her go'. ynteu then marks the change of subject to Llwyd. y trewis 'struck', 3 sg. preterite of taraw. hudlath 'magic wand': hut + llath 'rod', softened in the compound. y datrithwys 'he un-transformed', 3 sg. preterite of datrithaw (dat- 'un-' + rithaw). yn wreigyang ← gwreigyang 'young woman' (gwreic + ieuanc), softened after yn. geccaf: Evans reads geccaf (the g is certain on the image), where the second witness and the Red Book have deccaf 'fairest' (teccaf, softened after the feminine noun). It is a readable slip, kept and glossed as deccaf. The witness's asterisk before a welsei is dropped; nothing is missing (the Red Book has nothing there either). a welsei neb 'that anyone had seen': welsei is the pluperfect.

sentences.t: “Edrych i'th gylch ar y wlat,” heb ef, “a thi a wely yr holl anhedeu, a'r kyuanhed, ual y buant oreu.”
sentences.l: “Look in your circle at the land,” said he, “and you it-is-that will-see all the dwellings, and the settlement, as they-were best.”
sentences.i: “Look around you at the land,” he said, “and you will see all the dwellings and the settled country as they were at their best.”
sentences.n: Edrych 'look', 2 sg. imperative. i'th gylch 'around you' ← kylch 'circle', softened after 'th. a thi a wely 'and you will see' (gwely softened after a; thi ← ti, spirant after a). anhedeu 'dwellings' (anhed). kyuanhed 'settled, inhabited land'. ual y buant oreu 'as they were best' ← goreu, softened as an adverb.

sentences.t: Ac yna kyuodi a oruc ynteu ac edrych.
sentences.l: And then rising he-did he-for-his-part, and looking.
sentences.i: And then he rose and looked.
sentences.n: kyuodi a oruc … ac edrych: the second verbal noun follows the a oruc and takes its sense from it.

sentences.t: A phan edrych, ef a welei yr holl wlat yn gyuanhed, ac yn gyweir o'y holl alauoed a'y hanedeu.
sentences.l: And when he-looks, he it-was-that saw the whole land inhabited, and furnished with its all herds and its dwellings.
sentences.i: And when he looked, he saw the whole land settled again, and well stocked with all its herds and dwellings.
sentences.n: pan edrych 'when he looks', the bare stem as 3 sg. present; the Red Book has the preterite, a phan edrychawd ef. ef a welei 'he saw' (imperfect, softened after a). yn gyuanhed 'inhabited' ← kyuanhed, softened after yn. yn gyweir ← kyweir 'furnished, in order'. o'y holl alauoed 'with all its herds': alauoed, plural of alaw 'wealth in cattle'; o'y is o + 'y 'her' (gwlat is feminine). a'y hanedeu 'and its dwellings' ← anedeu: 'y 'her' puts h before a vowel.

sentences.t: “Pa ryw wassanaeth y bu Pryderi a Riannon yndaw?” heb ef.
sentences.l: “What kind of service were Pryderi and Rhiannon in-it?” said he.
sentences.i: “What sort of service were Pryderi and Rhiannon held in?” he said.
sentences.n: Pa ryw wassanaeth ← gwassanaeth 'service', softened after ryw. y bu 'were': a singular verb with a plural subject that follows it, as is usual in Middle Welsh. yndaw 'in it'.

sentences.t: “Pryderi a uydei ac yrd porth uy llys i am y uynwgyl, a Riannon a uydei a mynweireu yr essynn, wedy bydyn yn kywein gueir, am y mynwgyl hitheu. Ac yuelly y bu eu carchar.”
sentences.l: “Pryderi it-was-that used-to-be with the hammers of-the gate of my court I about his neck, and Rhiannon it-was-that used-to-be with the collars of the asses, after they-had-been carting hay, about her neck she-for-her-part. And thus was their imprisonment.”
sentences.i: “Pryderi used to wear the gate-hammers of my court about his neck, and Rhiannon about hers the collars of the asses, after they had been hauling hay. And such was their imprisonment.”
sentences.n: a uydei 'used to be' ← bydei, 3 sg. habitual imperfect of bot, softened after a. yrd, plural of ord 'sledge-hammer'. yrd porth 'gate-hammers' is not further explained: whether they were knockers or mallets kept at the gate is not certain. uy llys i 'my court': ll does not take the nasal. am y uynwgyl 'about his neck' ← mynwgyl, softened after y 'his'; contrast am y mynwgyl hitheu 'about her neck', unsoftened after y 'her', with hitheu making the 'her' plain. mynweireu 'collars' (mwn 'neck' + gweir 'band'). yr essynn 'of the asses', plural of assyn. wedy bydyn: so Evans and the second witness; the Red Book has bydynt. It is either a slip for bydynt (3 pl. habitual imperfect of bot, 'after they had been') or a 3 pl. form without the -t. yn kywein gueir: so Evans; the Red Book has kywein geir. The sense is uncertain. The likeliest reading is kywein 'carry, cart in (a harvest)' (modern cywain) with gueir 'hay' (gwair), 'carting hay', but the meaning of kywein here is not secure. bu eu carchar 'was their imprisonment'.

sentences.t: Ac o achaws y carchar hwnnw, y gelwit y kyuarwydyt hwnnw, Mabinogi Mynweir a Mynord.
sentences.l: And because-of that imprisonment, was-called that tale the Mabinogi of Collar and Hammer.
sentences.i: And because of that imprisonment, this tale was called the Mabinogi of the Collar and the Hammer.
sentences.n: o achaws 'because of'. y gelwit 'was called': gelwit is the impersonal imperfect (-it) of galw. y kyuarwydyt hwnnw 'that tale' (kyuarwydyt 'lore, story', as in 007). Mynweir a Mynord: so Evans; the Red Book has mynnweir a mynoad. mynweir is the 'collar' of 99. mynord seems to be mwn 'neck' + ord 'hammer', a hammer worn on the neck, which answers to Pryderi's yrd. The Red Book's mynoad is a different form whose sense is not clear.

sentences.t: Ac yuelly y teruyna y geing honn yma o'r Mabinogy.
sentences.l: And thus ends this branch here of the Mabinogi.
sentences.i: And thus ends this branch of the Mabinogi.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of the First Branch. teruyna 'ends', 3 sg. present of teruynu. y geing honn 'this branch': keing, softened after the article (feminine). Evans has geing here; the Red Book has geinc. Mabinogy: so written, with final y; the Red Book has mabinogi.
